note: Ten recordings of bird song from xeno-canto, all licensed CC BY-SA by their recordists (licence read on each recording's xeno-canto page on 2026-11-19). The canon column is the human rendering of the song as a published source prints it, quoted verbatim; sources fetched 2026-11-19. Keys a..j are the order in which the songs were listed here, before any spectrogram was drawn.

songs.canon_quote: The classic Eastern Towhee song, given by males, is a loud drink-your-tea! lasting about 1 second.

songs.canon: Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?
songs.canon_quote: Barred Owls have a distinctive hooting call of 8–9 notes, described as "Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?"
White-throated Sparrows sing a pretty, thin whistle that sounds like Oh-sweet-canada-canada or Old-Sam-Peabody-Peabody.
The primary mating and territorial song of the male Ovenbird is a rapid, resounding tea-cher, Tea-cher, TEA-cher growing louder over the first few repetitions, with 8 to 13 teacher phrases in all.
The song most often heard is a short ditty often described as Pleased, pleased, pleased to meetcha! or I wish to meet Miss Beecher!
In most of North America, the song is a simple, pure 2 or 3-note whistled fee-bee or hey, sweetie.
Males sing a burry rreeee-BEEP or free-beer!, reminiscent of but thinner than an Eastern Phoebe's song.

songs.canon: sweet sweet sweet I'm so sweet
songs.canon_quote: The tone is so sweet that people often remember it with the mnemonic sweet sweet sweet I'm so sweet.

songs.canon: cheer, cheer, cheer / birdie, birdie, birdie
songs.canon_quote: Syllables can sound like the bird is singing cheer, cheer, cheer or birdie, birdie, birdie.

songs.canon: Spit. And see if I care. Spit. / Pik-chicka-weew
songs.canon_quote: Some suggest that they sing Spit. And see if I care. Spit. while others suggest they sing Pik-chicka-weew.
